t:
Section 175 of title 28, United States Code, in its present form is stricken, and the following section is inserted as section 175 of title 28 of the United States Code:


“§ 175. Assignment of judges; divisions; hearings; quorum; decisions
“(a) Judges of the Court of Claims shall sit on the court and its divisions in such order and at such times as the court directs.
“(b) The Court of Claims may authorize the hearing and determination of cases and controversies by separate divisions, each consisting of three judges. Such divisions shall sit at the times and places and hear the cases and controversies assigned as the court directs.
“(c) Cases and controversies shall be heard and determined by a court or division of not more than three judges, unless a hearing en banc is ordered by the court or by the chief judge. The court en banc for an initial hearing shall consist of the judges of the Court of Claims in regular active service. In case of a vacancy in the court or of the inability of a judge thereof in regular active service to sit, a justice or judge assigned to the court pursuant to chapter 13 of this title shall be competent to sit in the court en banc when designated by the court to do so.
“(d) A rehearing en banc may be ordered by a majority of the judges of the Court of Claims in regular active service. The court en banc for a rehearing shall consist of the judges of the Court of Claims in regular active service. A judge of the Court of Claims who has retired from regular active service shall also be competent to sit as a judge of the court en banc in the rehearing of a case or controversy if he sat on the court or division at the original hearing thereof.
“(e) Two judges shall constitute a quorum of a division of the Court of Claims, four judges shall constitute a quorum of a court en banc.
“(f) A majority of the judges or justices who actually sit on the court or division or court en banc must concur in any decision.”

fable.w: The tempting reading is that references to a "hearing" and to "cases and controversies" signal public hearings or a right to sue the government. The section only sets out the internal organisation of the Court of Claims: assignment of judges, divisions, en banc procedure, quorum and concurrence. It does not grant any outside party a right to sue or require consultation with anyone outside the federal government, since every actor is a federal judge. Describing how a court sits is not the same as granting participation in a federal decision.
fable.s: The Court of Claims may authorize the hearing and determination of cases and controversies by separate divisions, each consisting of three judges.

qwen_block.w: This section outlines the internal procedural rules for the Court of Claims, specifically regarding the assignment of judges, quorum requirements, and decision-making processes. All actors involved (judges, the court itself) are part of the federal government. There is no requirement for consultation with or participation by outside parties such as the public, states, or private entities.
qwen_block.s: Judges of the Court of Claims shall sit on the court and its divisions in such order and at such times as the court directs.

opus.w: This section only sets out how the Court of Claims is organized internally: judge assignments, three-judge divisions, en banc hearings, quorum and the votes needed for a decision. Everyone involved is a federal judge or justice, so nothing crosses the federal boundary. The word "hearing" here means a court hearing a case, not a public hearing or comment process, and describing how a court works is not the same as granting outsiders a right to sue over a decision.
opus.s: The Court of Claims may authorize the hearing and determination of cases and controversies by separate divisions, each consisting of three judges.
opus.b: Step 1, the tempting reading: the section keeps using the words "hearing," "rehearing en banc" and "decisions," which could look like a public hearing before a federal decision. That fails the definition. These are court hearings of cases, and the section only covers how the Court of Claims arranges its own federal judges: assignments, three-judge divisions, en banc sittings, quorum and voting. Every actor is a federal judge or justice. The section does not give any outside party a new right to sue or to take part in a federal decision. It only describes how the court is organized, which the definition treats as "No."

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines the internal procedural rules and composition of the Court of Claims, including quorum requirements and how judges are assigned. It does not require the federal government to consult with outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) before making a decision. The definition of participation excludes the mere description of court jurisdiction or procedural mechanics, and the actors involved in these decisions (judges) are federal officials.
qwen_chat.s: “(a) Judges of the Court of Claims shall sit on the court and its divisions in such order and at such times as the court directs. ... (e) Two judges shall constitute a quorum of a division of the Court of Claims, four judges shall constitute a quorum of a court en banc. (f) A majority of the judges or justices who actually sit on the court or division or court en banc must concur in any decision.”
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Court of Claims hears cases involving private parties (plaintiffs suing the government), this constitutes participation. However, the definition explicitly excludes "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits" and distinguishes between granting a right to sue and the procedural mechanics of the court itself. This section describes the internal administrative structure of the court (quorums, divisions, en banc hearings), not a mechanism for outside parties to consult with the government before a decision is made. The "participation" definition requires consultation or coordination *before* a decision, or an advisory role. Judicial proceedings are adversarial, not consultative in the sense defined. Furthermore, the actors involved in the decision-making process described here (judges) are federal officials.
